questions.question: Which statement best captures the core invariant of a production Transformer service?
options: Every GPU should remain at 100% utilization at all times.
Every request should use the largest available context window.
Admitted work must fit the declared memory, latency, correctness, and availability envelope.
Every model must use tensor and pipeline parallelism together.
questions.explanation: Utilization is secondary. Admission must preserve the service contract across memory, latency, correctness, and availability.

questions.question: Why should time to first token and inter-token latency be measured separately?
options: They represent different phases: queueing and prefill versus repeated decode cadence.
Only inter-token latency includes tokenization.
Time to first token is always lower than one decode step.
They are identical whenever continuous batching is enabled.
questions.explanation: TTFT includes admission, queueing, and prefill, while inter-token latency describes the cadence of subsequent decode iterations.

questions.question: A 32-layer decoder uses 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, and 2-byte cache elements. How much KV state does one cached token require across all layers?
options: 8 KiB
128 KiB
2 MiB
8 MiB
questions.explanation: Keys and values require 2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes, or 128 KiB, per cached token.

questions.question: What changes when an MHA checkpoint is replaced by a compatible GQA checkpoint?
options: The causal mask becomes bidirectional.
Several query heads share each key and value head, reducing KV-cache state.
All feed-forward layers are removed.
The server no longer needs KV cache during decode.
questions.explanation: GQA groups query heads around fewer KV heads. That reduces cache and bandwidth, but it is a learned checkpoint shape rather than a free server toggle.

questions.question: When is tensor parallelism most directly justified for inference?
options: When independent replicas already fit and communication is the bottleneck.
When one request should be sent to two unrelated model versions.
When layer weights or live state need to be partitioned across tightly connected devices.
When the tokenizer produces too many vocabulary entries.
questions.explanation: Tensor parallelism shards layer operations and their state. It can solve per-device fit or compute pressure, at the cost of token-path collectives.

questions.question: Why can continuous batching outperform a static request batch for mixed generation lengths?
options: It lets the model look at future tokens.
It replaces completed sequences with compatible queued work at iteration boundaries.
It stores model weights only while a request is active.
It guarantees that no request will ever queue.
questions.explanation: Continuous batching avoids leaving early-finished slots idle until the longest request in a static batch completes.

questions.question: A four-GPU serving group loses one required GPU. What is the safest immediate assumption?
options: The remaining three GPUs can always continue the same topology.
Only output quality is affected; capacity is unchanged.
The group is unavailable until the required shards and communication topology are restored or replaced.
Admission should increase to keep the remaining GPUs busy.
questions.explanation: A sharded replica depends on all required ranks. Admission should move to another healthy group or reject boundedly rather than using a partial topology.

questions.question: Which release test is most likely to reveal that a faster kernel is unsafe?
options: A throughput-only benchmark with one short prompt.
A correctness and quality comparison using the exact checkpoint, tokenizer, precision, masks, and runtime bundle.
A count of how many source files changed.
A GPU utilization screenshot without request traces.
questions.explanation: Kernel and precision changes must preserve the exact model contract and output-quality criteria, not only improve raw speed.
